title: Does the top bid get the top ad?
hook: Ad A bids more per click than ad B. Is A sure to get the top slot?

knows: ads can be sold by auction
doesNotKnow: that when ads are ranked by bid times a quality score, a lower bid can win the top slot and pay less

misconception: The highest bidder always gets the top ad slot.
objective: The learner can rank two ads by bid × quality, see that the lower bid can come first, and work out that under a pay-the-least-that-keeps-your-rank rule the winner pays the next ad's score divided by its own quality.

claims.text: Ranked by bid alone, A's $2.00 beats B's $1.50 and takes the top slot.
claims.source: 2.00 > 1.50; Demo.tsx key(…, 'bid'). | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. In bid mode, key = round(bid x 1000): A 2000 > B 1500, so A is top. The Demo shows 'Ranked by bid alone.' and the Top slot readout 'Ad A'. The reveal's 'A's $2.00 took the top' matches.

claims.text: Ranked by bid × quality, B scores $1.50 × 1.0 = 1.5 and A scores $2.00 × 0.5 = 1.0, so B takes the top slot with the lower bid.
claims.source: Arithmetic; Demo.tsx key(…, 'score'). Brief check in company/domains/briefs/economics.markets.md #22. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own copy of key() in score mode: B 1.5 x 1.0 = 1.5 (1500) > A 2.0 x 0.5 = 1.0 (1000), so B is top. The reveal prints '$1.50 x 1.0 = 1.5 against A's $2.00 x 0.5 = 1.0'; the predict key 'Ad B' matches.

claims.text: Under the rule 'the top ad pays the least bid that keeps its slot', the top ad pays the next score ÷ its own quality: B pays 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = $1.00 a click, less than A bid, and still $1.00 when B bids $1.20, because A's score sets it, not B's bid. (Stage: 'B pays A's score 1.0 ÷ B's quality 1.0.')
claims.source: B stays on top for any bid above A's score ÷ B's quality = 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = $1.00 (equal at $1.00); price = next score ÷ own quality. Demo.tsx B_PRICE. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Demo pays = second.bid x second.quality / top.quality = 1.0 / 1.0 = $1.00, the same for B at $1.50 and at $1.20 (own node), and B_PRICE = A_SCORE / B_QUALITY = 1.00. $1.00 < A's $2.00 bid. 'Least bid that keeps your slot' is the usual GSP boundary: equal at $1.00, as the source says, and the chip states the rule. | REWORDED v2 (builder, 2026-10-14): Adds the general form (next score ÷ own quality) and the $1.20 case, both shown on stage in the working line and the price log. Same arithmetic as pass 23 (Demo pays = second.bid x second.quality / top.quality). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node with the Demo's integer keys: B at $1.50 and $1.20 tops (1500, 1200 > 1000) and pays 1.0 / 1.0 = $1.00. Every reachable log order checked: the reveal names the first B-on-top bid tried, or 'on top, B pays' if none was tried in score mode.

claims.text: With B's bid at $0.80, B's score 0.8 falls below A's 1.0 and A takes the top slot back and pays 0.8 ÷ 0.5 = $1.60 a click: dividing by A's quality 0.5 doubles it. At $1.00 the two tie.
claims.source: 0.80 × 1.0 = 0.8 < 1.0; 0.8 ÷ 0.5 = 1.60; 1.00 × 1.0 = 1.0 = 2.00 × 0.5. Demo.tsx readouts. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node with the Demo's integer keys. B $0.80: 800 < 1000, so A is top and pays 0.8 x 1.0 / 0.5 = $1.60. B $1.00: 1000 = 1000, so the readout says 'Tie' and pays shows a dash. The milestone a-retakes is reachable only at $0.80 in score mode, so the reveal's 'When you dropped B to $0.80' quotes a state the learner reached. (At a tie the stage draws A in the top row while the readout says Tie; that is cosmetic, not a claim.) | REWORDED v2 (builder, 2026-10-14): The $1.60 case is now quoted in the reveal (from the learner's price log) and its working is on stage. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node: B $0.80 -> key 800 < 1000, A tops, pays 0.8 x 1.0 / 0.5 = $1.60; B $1.00 -> 1000 = 1000, Tie. Milestone a-retakes guarantees the $0.80 log entry exists.

claims.text: The ranking and payment rule are a simplified model with invented numbers, not a description of any real search engine.
claims.source: Stage chip states the payment rule; reveal footnote. The brief's planned claim about real search engines (quality factor used, formulas not public; E&K ch. 15) needs a human source check and is kept out of learner text. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Chip 'Model: the top ad pays the least bid that keeps its slot'; the reveal footnote is word for word this claim. The real-search-engine claim from the brief is kept out of learner text, as the source says; I checked every learner string in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: Quality multiplies the bid, so A, at half B's quality, would need more than $3.00 to beat B's $1.50.
claims.source: UNRECORDED CLAIM found by fact-checker (pass 23, 2026-10-14); the sentence is the builder's, recorded here word for word. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. Reveal para 2, last sentence (line 62). Under the lesson's own rule (rank by bid x quality) it is false: A, at quality 0.5, outranks B's 1.5 with any bid above $3.00 (e.g. $3.10 x 0.5 = 1.55). A higher bid compensates for lower quality at a rate of 1/quality; that is the point of the score. The stage only varies B's bid, so the learner never tests this, but the sentence is stated generally. Fix (builder): 'A high bid alone does not win: A would need more than $3.00, double B's $1.50, because its quality is half B's.' Or 'Quality multiplies the bid, so a low-quality ad has to bid much more to win.' | REWORDED v2 (builder, 2026-10-14): Was 'A high bid cannot make up for low quality' (disputed pass 23: false under the lesson's own rule). Reworded per the fact-checker's suggested fix: A's score 0.5 x bid > 1.5 needs bid > $3.00. Told, not shown (the stage varies only B's bid). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Rank by bid x quality: A's score 0.5 x bid > B's 1.5 iff bid > $3.00 (own node: $3.00 ties at 1500, $3.01 gives 1505). Reveal computes usd(1.5 x 1.0 / 0.5) = $3.00. Pass 23 dispute resolved: the new wording is true under the lesson's rule.

recall.question: Ads are ranked by bid × quality. Ad P bids $3 with quality 0.4; ad Q bids $2 with quality 0.8. Which ad is ranked first?
recall.why: P scores 3 × 0.4 = 1.2 and Q scores 2 × 0.8 = 1.6. The product decides, so the lower bid can win.
